# Diagnosing P055B on the 2014 Chevy Impala: Locating Sensor B

When a vehicle throws a P055b code—Engine oil pressure sensor/switch "B" circuit range/performance—the immediate assumption is often that a single component has failed. However, in the context of General Motors' Ecotec engine family found in the 2014 Impala LS, this error points to a specific duality within the lubrication monitoring system. Understanding the physical layout and electrical logic of these sensors is critical before ordering parts or attempting disassembly.

On the 2.5L Ecotec inline-four used in your model year, there are indeed two distinct oil pressure sensing devices. The sensor you have already located on top of the engine block, near the intake manifold solenoid and circled in red in your visual reference, is Sensor A (or Sensor 1). This unit typically monitors raw crankcase pressure and sends a signal directly to the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) via a single wire. It serves as the primary gauge for mechanical oil pressure throughout the lubrication circuit.

The elusive "Sensor B" referenced in the P055b code is not located on the engine block itself. Instead, it resides inside the instrument cluster. This design creates a redundant monitoring loop where Sensor A handles the raw data acquisition from the engine bay, while Sensor B acts as the receiver and comparator within the dash assembly. The PCM expects a specific voltage correlation between these two points. If the signal from the engine-mounted sensor (A) does not match the expected parameters relative to the cluster sensor's input, or if there is an open circuit in the wiring harness connecting them, the PCM logs P055b.

This architecture presents a common diagnostic pitfall. Technicians often replace the external sensor expecting it to resolve the fault, only for the code to persist because the issue lies with the internal cluster unit or the wiring loom running from the firewall to the dash. When diagnosing this specific code, you must verify continuity on the harness between the engine block connector and the instrument cluster connector. A multimeter test is necessary; check for 12V at the sensor location and ensure ground paths are intact before condemning the external unit.

If the wiring checks out clean and the dipstick confirms adequate oil volume, the failure is likely a bad internal switch within the instrument panel or a corrupted PCM calibration of the expected range. In this scenario, replacing just Sensor A will yield no results. The repair involves either reprogramming the cluster (if supported by the specific model year's flash capabilities) or swapping the entire instrument cluster assembly to restore the correct voltage correlation between Sensor A and Sensor B.

From an engineering perspective, this redundancy is a safety feature designed to prevent false low-oil-pressure warnings that could lead to unnecessary panic stops, while simultaneously ensuring that if one sensor fails completely, the other provides a backup state for the driver or the PCM's fail-safe mode. However, it complicates DIY repairs by obscuring the location of the faulty component until a thorough electrical diagnosis is performed. Always verify the circuit range and performance against known good data before assuming a simple part replacement will solve the problem.
